results.text:
Figure 3.7
Scatter plot titled “Low- and middle-income countries are exposed to similar levels of risk from climate change, and they have less adaptive capacity.” The x-axis is Exposure index (higher scores indicate greater risk), scaled from 0 to 0.8. Three country-income groups are shown with colored dots and separate solid linear trend lines: Low-income (dark navy), Middle-income (orange), and High-income (teal). The low-income group clusters mostly around exposure roughly 0.35–0.55 and adaptive capacity roughly 0.65–0.87, with an upward-sloping trend line. The middle-income group clusters mainly around exposure roughly 0.25–0.58 and adaptive capacity roughly 0.35–0.78, with a moderately upward-sloping trend line; one visible orange point lies near exposure about 0.71 and adaptive capacity about 0.50. The high-income group clusters mainly around exposure roughly 0.26–0.58 and adaptive capacity roughly 0.18–0.62, with a nearly flat but slightly upward-sloping trend line. Source note: WDR 2024 team using data from ND-GAIN Country Index (University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Index) dashboard, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN, https://gain.nd.edu/our-work/country-index/. Note: The solid lines show the linear relationship for each country group.

results.text:
Figure 1.1
Scatter plot showing economies’ GNI per capita in 1990 (x-axis) versus 2022 (y-axis), both in current US dollars. Title: “A handful of economies have transitioned from middle-income to high-income status over the last three decades.” The plot covers x from 0 to 10,000 and y from 0 to 45,000, with light horizontal gridlines and labeled income-group bands. Blue vertical threshold lines mark 1990 income-class cutoffs at US$610 (transition to lower-middle-income), US$2,465 (transition to upper-middle-income), and US$7,620 (transition to high-income). Blue horizontal threshold lines mark the corresponding 2022 cutoffs at US$1,135, US$4,465, and US$13,845. Income-group labels appear across the top as Low-income, Lower-middle-income, Upper-middle-income, High-income, and along the right side as Lower-middle-income, Upper-middle-income, High-income. Orange scatter points represent economies; many are unlabeled, while labeled high/upper-middle economies include GUY, ROM, CHL, PAN, TTO, SYC, PRI, PRT, KNA, OMN, GRC, ATG, BRB, BHR, CZE, EST, LTU, LVA, SVK, HRV, POL, HUN, URY, SVN, MLT, KOR, SAU, and MAC. The labeled points show substantial upward movement for a small set of economies, with MAC highest near 2022 GNI per capita of about US$45,000 and 1990 GNI per capita around US$9,000; KOR is near US$36,000 in 2022 and about US$6,500 in 1990; MLT and SVN are above US$30,000 in 2022; and several economies cluster around the upper-middle/high-income boundary. Source note: WDR 2024 team using WDI (World Development Indicators), World Bank. Note says each point is an economy’s 1990 and 2022 GNI per capita using the World Bank Atlas method; the figure includes only economies at middle-income levels in 1990; only economies that transitioned to high-income status since 1990 are labeled; 1990 data were unavailable for six economies.

results.text:
Map 6.2
Limited or outdated electricity transmission networks serve as barriers to the entry of renewable sources. World map showing electricity transmission networks in 2023. Power transmission lines are drawn as thin red/orange line segments across regions. Coverage is dense in North America, Europe, India, eastern China, parts of South America, southern Africa, and Australia; much sparser across much of Africa, the Middle East, and interior regions of some continents. Two boxed callouts mark areas for enlargement: 'See inset map A for more detail' over Europe / North Africa / West Asia, and 'See inset map B for more detail' over East Asia. Inset map A at lower left shows a denser close-up of transmission lines across Europe and adjacent regions. Inset map B at right shows a close-up of East Asia, especially China and neighboring areas, with dense transmission lines. Legend at lower left labels the line symbol as 'Power transmission lines.' Source credited to Arkolakis and Walsh 2023; note states the map displays electricity transmission networks in 2023 and the two insets focus on areas of particular interest due to geographic disparities in coverage of transmission networks in these regions.

Figure 5.1
Stacked bar chart titled "The share of skilled workers in large firms increases with GDP per capita." Vertical axis: "Share of workers (%)" from 0 to 100. Horizontal axis: four categories, "Country income group 1," "Country income group 2," "Country income group 3," and "Country income group 4." Each bar is a 100% stack with six legend categories: gray = Small firms, low skills; orange = Small firms, high skills; teal = Medium firms, low skills; gold = Medium firms, high skills; dark blue = Large firms, low skills; olive green = Large firms, high skills. Visually, the share in small firms with low skills is largest in country income group 1 and declines steadily across groups; the share in large firms with high skills rises steadily and is largest in country income group 4. Approximate visible composition by group: group 1 has about half small-firm low-skill workers, with the remaining half split across the other five categories; group 2 shows a smaller gray segment and a noticeably larger olive segment; group 3 and group 4 are increasingly dominated by medium/large firm and high-skill segments, especially olive green (large firms, high skills). Source: Gottlieb, Poschke, and Tueting 2024. Note states that the figure shows the share of low-skilled and highly skilled workers employed in small, medium, and large firms across four country income categories corresponding to GDP per capita levels of US$0–US$3,000 (group 1), US$3,000–US$10,000 (group 2), US$10,000–US$30,000 (group 3), and more than US$30,000 (group 4). Shares are computed from nationally representative labor force surveys from 76 countries covering 805 country-years. Small firms have fewer than 10 employees; medium firms have 10–50 employees; large firms have more than 50 employees. Workers are classified as low-skilled if they have less than nine years of formal education and as highly skilled otherwise. For countries in each income group, the bars add up to 100 percent.

Figure 7.5
Horizontal grouped bar chart titled: "In middle-income countries, both economywide and sectoral input and product market regulations are more restrictive than in high-income countries." Source note visible beneath the chart cites WDR 2024 team using PMR Database / OECD-WBG Product Market Regulation Database and OECD PMR Indicators; note explains PMR ranges from 0 to 6 and lower values indicate more competition-friendly regulation, with data for 38 high-income and 22 middle-income countries.

context.text:
Figure 3.7
Scatter plot titled “Low- and middle-income countries are exposed to similar levels of risk from climate change, and they have less adaptive capacity.” The x-axis is Exposure index (higher scores indicate greater risk), scaled from 0 to 0.8. The y-axis is Adaptive capacity index (higher scores indicate lower capacity), scaled from 0 to 1.0. Three country-income groups are shown with colored dots and separate solid linear trend lines: Low-income (dark navy), Middle-income (orange), and High-income (teal). The low-income group clusters mostly around exposure roughly 0.35–0.55 and adaptive capacity roughly 0.65–0.87, with an upward-sloping trend line. The middle-income group clusters mainly around exposure roughly 0.25–0.58 and adaptive capacity roughly 0.35–0.78, with a moderately upward-sloping trend line; one visible orange point lies near exposure about 0.71 and adaptive capacity about 0.50. The high-income group clusters mainly around exposure roughly 0.26–0.58 and adaptive capacity roughly 0.18–0.62, with a nearly flat but slightly upward-sloping trend line. Source note: WDR 2024 team using data from ND-GAIN Country Index (University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Index) dashboard, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN, https://gain.nd.edu/our-work/country-index/. Note: The solid lines show the linear relationship for each country group.

Figure 6.7
Figure 6.7. Most of the countries currently “locked in” to declining brown industries are middle-income countries. Composite figure with two panels. Panel a: bar chart titled “Brown Lock-in Index for top 10 highest-risk middle-income countries.” Y-axis is Brown Lock-in Index, ranging from 0 to 3.5. Ten countries on the x-axis, with approximate bar heights (highest to lowest): Iraq (~3.45), Libya (~3.25), Angola (~3.25), Equatorial Guinea (~3.20), Azerbaijan (~3.18), Nigeria (~3.17), Algeria (~2.90), Turkmenistan (~2.48), Timor-Leste (~2.25), Gabon (~2.20). Panel b: scatter plot titled “Brown Lock-in Index versus Transition Outlook for middle-income countries.” X-axis is Brown Lock-in Index (about -1.0 to 4.0); Y-axis is Transition Outlook (about -3.0 to 2.5). Points are color-coded by income group, with legend: Lower-middle-income (teal) and Upper-middle-income (orange). Dashed reference lines cross at approximately x=0 and y=0. Country abbreviations are plotted as labeled points; visible labels include KHM, VUT, LCA, VCT, MDV, BLR, TKM, IRQ, SWZ, NAM, TUV, UZB, EGY, BRA, IDN, MMR, CIV, ARG, GHA, MNG, ECU, RUS, IRN, KAZ, COL, DZA, AZE, CMR, NGA, PNG, AGO, GNQ, TLS, LBY, GAB, BOL, COG, NIC, MRT, and others clustered near the origin. The general pattern shows many countries clustered at low Brown Lock-in Index values near the left side, with several high-lock-in countries on the far right, often with negative Transition Outlook. Source note in the figure cites WDR 2024 team analysis based on Andres et al. (2023) and defines Brown Lock-in Index and Transition Outlook.

Figure 1.1
Scatter plot showing economies’ GNI per capita in 1990 (x-axis) versus 2022 (y-axis), both in current US dollars. Title: “A handful of economies have transitioned from middle-income to high-income status over the last three decades.” The plot covers x from 0 to 10,000 and y from 0 to 45,000, with light horizontal gridlines and labeled income-group bands. Blue vertical threshold lines mark 1990 income-class cutoffs at US$610 (transition to lower-middle-income), US$2,465 (transition to upper-middle-income), and US$7,620 (transition to high-income). Blue horizontal threshold lines mark the corresponding 2022 cutoffs at US$1,135, US$4,465, and US$13,845. Income-group labels appear across the top as Low-income, Lower-middle-income, Upper-middle-income, High-income, and along the right side as Lower-middle-income, Upper-middle-income, High-income. Orange scatter points represent economies; many are unlabeled, while labeled high/upper-middle economies include GUY, ROM, CHL, PAN, TTO, SYC, PRI, PRT, KNA, OMN, GRC, ATG, BRB, BHR, CZE, EST, LTU, LVA, SVK, HRV, POL, HUN, URY, SVN, MLT, KOR, SAU, and MAC. The labeled points show substantial upward movement for a small set of economies, with MAC highest near 2022 GNI per capita of about US$45,000 and 1990 GNI per capita around US$9,000; KOR is near US$36,000 in 2022 and about US$6,500 in 1990; MLT and SVN are above US$30,000 in 2022; and several economies cluster around the upper-middle/high-income boundary. Source note: WDR 2024 team using WDI (World Development Indicators), World Bank. Note says each point is an economy’s 1990 and 2022 GNI per capita using the World Bank Atlas method; the figure includes only economies at middle-income levels in 1990; only economies that transitioned to high-income status since 1990 are labeled; 1990 data were unavailable for six economies.

Map 6.2
Limited or outdated electricity transmission networks serve as barriers to the entry of renewable sources. World map showing electricity transmission networks in 2023. Power transmission lines are drawn as thin red/orange line segments across regions. Coverage is dense in North America, Europe, India, eastern China, parts of South America, southern Africa, and Australia; much sparser across much of Africa, the Middle East, and interior regions of some continents. Two boxed callouts mark areas for enlargement: 'See inset map A for more detail' over Europe / North Africa / West Asia, and 'See inset map B for more detail' over East Asia. Inset map A at lower left shows a denser close-up of transmission lines across Europe and adjacent regions. Inset map B at right shows a close-up of East Asia, especially China and neighboring areas, with dense transmission lines. Legend at lower left labels the line symbol as 'Power transmission lines.' Source credited to Arkolakis and Walsh 2023; note states the map displays electricity transmission networks in 2023 and the two insets focus on areas of particular interest due to geographic disparities in coverage of transmission networks in these regions.

Figure 5.1
Stacked bar chart titled "The share of skilled workers in large firms increases with GDP per capita." Vertical axis: "Share of workers (%)" from 0 to 100. Horizontal axis: four categories, "Country income group 1," "Country income group 2," "Country income group 3," and "Country income group 4." Each bar is a 100% stack with six legend categories: gray = Small firms, low skills; orange = Small firms, high skills; teal = Medium firms, low skills; gold = Medium firms, high skills; dark blue = Large firms, low skills; olive green = Large firms, high skills. Visually, the share in small firms with low skills is largest in country income group 1 and declines steadily across groups; the share in large firms with high skills rises steadily and is largest in country income group 4. Approximate visible composition by group: group 1 has about half small-firm low-skill workers, with the remaining half split across the other five categories; group 2 shows a smaller gray segment and a noticeably larger olive segment; group 3 and group 4 are increasingly dominated by medium/large firm and high-skill segments, especially olive green (large firms, high skills). Source: Gottlieb, Poschke, and Tueting 2024. Note states that the figure shows the share of low-skilled and highly skilled workers employed in small, medium, and large firms across four country income categories corresponding to GDP per capita levels of US$0–US$3,000 (group 1), US$3,000–US$10,000 (group 2), US$10,000–US$30,000 (group 3), and more than US$30,000 (group 4). Shares are computed from nationally representative labor force surveys from 76 countries covering 805 country-years. Small firms have fewer than 10 employees; medium firms have 10–50 employees; large firms have more than 50 employees. Workers are classified as low-skilled if they have less than nine years of formal education and as highly skilled otherwise. For countries in each income group, the bars add up to 100 percent.

initial_ranking.text:
Figure O.1
Title: "Income per capita of middle-income countries relative to that of the United States has been stagnant for decades." 

Chart type: multi-series line chart.

X-axis: years 1970 to 2022.
Y-axis: "Share of US GNI per capita (%)" with tick marks from 0 to 60 in increments of 5.

Legend/series:
- Dark line: "Middle-income countries"
- Orange line: "Middle-income countries, excluding China"
- Light gray comparison lines labeled in the plot: "Korea, Rep.", "Poland", and "Chile"

Visible relationships/trends:
- The two aggregate middle-income-country series stay low relative to the United States, generally around the low single digits to about 8% over the period, with a modest rise after roughly 2008 and a slight easing after the mid-2010s.
- The "excluding China" series tracks slightly below the full middle-income-country series for most of the period.
- Korea, Rep. rises strongly from the mid-teens in the 1970s to just above 50% in the late 2010s/early 2020s, then remains near that level.
- Poland rises from around 10% in 1970 to the mid-20% range by 2022.
- Chile rises from roughly the low-to-mid teens in the late 1970s/1980s to about 20%+ by 2022.

Source: WDR 2024 team using data from WDI (World Development Indicators) (Data Catalog), World Bank, Washington, DC, https://datacatalog.worldbank.org/search/dataset/0037712.

Note: The plotted lines indicate the trend of average income per capita in middle-income countries and in middle-income countries, excluding China, relative to income per capita of the United States (considered the economic frontier country). Country definitions are based on the first World Development Report (World Bank 1978), in which low-income countries have gross national income (GNI) per capita of US$250 or less; middle-income countries have GNI per capita of more than US$250; and industrialized (high-income) countries consist of member countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, except for Greece, Portugal, Spain, and Türkiye, which are classified as middle-income countries.
